README files are a way to document the contents and structure of a folder, helping users locate the information they need. Please consider adding a README to each repository or including ‘README’ in the name of your overview document.

Code Comments

Missing Files

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In all code files, libraries/imports were loaded in one block.

Packages / Dependencies

Reproducible Environment

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 20 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

A script runs longer than our limit of 5 minutes.

  • runGCM.R
  • runHierarchicalGCM.R
  • runHierarchicalPrototype.R
  • runPrototype.R

State in the README how long each script runs. If some steps take hours, save their results (such as fitted models) to files, add those to the deposit, and let the script read them, so readers can check the rest without waiting.

Comparison with the paper

Of the 2 statistical tests reported in the paper, 0 were found in the output of the code. No script ran to the end, so most results were never produced.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 4 scripts: 0 ran without error, 0 errored, 4 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

As a proxy for the existence of such distinctive features, a separate group of participants provided ratings of the extent to which each rock image possessed a highly distinctive feature not present in other items in the set.

Also following Nosofsky et al. ( 2025), for simplicity in the analysis, we assumed that all participants were governed by the same parameter values, i.e., we did not attempt to account for individualparticipant differences.

Ethics approval statement:

Ethics approval.

The study was approved by the Indiana University Institutional Review Board.

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

PubPeer Comments

We checked 52 references with DOIs. No references with comments in PubPeer were found.

RetractionWatch

We checked 52 references with DOIs. No citations to articles in the RetractionWatch database were found.

We checked 52 references with DOIs. No citations to articles in the FLoRA database were found.

How Ethics Approval Check works

This module searches for statements of ethics approval, IRB approval, institutional review board approval, and related terms.

Patterns are designed to capture:

Human research committee names - Institutional Review Board / IRB (US standard) - Independent Ethics Committee / IEC (ICH-GCP international clinical trial term) - Ethical/Ethics Review Board (generic) - Ethics (Advisory/Review) Committee/Board/Panel/Sub-committee - Research Ethics Committee/Board/Panel (UK/Canada/Australia) - Medical Ethics Committee - Human Subjects/Research Committee / Human Research Ethics (Advisory) Panel - Committee for/on the Protection of Human Subjects - Committee on (Health) Research Ethics - Office of Research Ethics - Abbreviations: IEC, REC, REB, ERB, METC, DEC. REC/REB/ERB/DEC are short enough to collide with unrelated jargon (e.g. REC as a recognition-heuristic model abbreviation, DEC as a decision-task label, Reb as an author surname), so these four require an ethics/approval/committee/board/panel/institutional/ protocol word within ~30 characters in the same sentence. IRB and IEC are kept unconstrained as they are not observed to collide in practice. - Dutch: Medisch-ethische toetsingscommissie (METC) - French: Comité d'éthique / Comité d'Ethique

Animal research committee names - Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee / IACUC (US standard) - Any sentence containing animal(s) and committee (or board/panel) within ~5 words of each other — catches Experimental Animal Care and Use Committee, Animal Ethics Committee, Animal Welfare Board, Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body, etc. - UK: Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body / AWERB - Dutch: Dierexperimentencommissie / DEC (see DEC constraint above); Instantie voor Dierenwelzijn / IvD - German: Tierversuchskommission / TvK (advisory committee under §15 Tierschutzgesetz) - French: Comité d'éthique en expérimentation animale / CEEA; Comité d'éthique animale - Spanish: Comité de ética en experimentación animal / CEEA

Approval phrasing - Ethics/Ethical (approval|clearance) [was] (granted|obtained|received|given|secured) - Ethically approved - Approved by the (ethics|irb|institutional|independent|local|review|research) ... - This/The study/protocol/experiment/procedures/methods/research [was] (approved|reviewed) by - Study was ethically approved - (Followed|met|follow) the ethical (guidelines|standards|requirements) - In accordance with ... ethical (guidelines|standards) - Ethics protocol - Approved under (protocol|reference|number)

Waiver / exemption - Ethics/Ethical (waiver|exemption) - IRB (waiver|exemption|exempt) - Exempted from (ethics|irb|institutional review) - Waived by the (ethics|irb|institutional|review) (committee|board) - Deemed exempt

Declaration of Helsinki - Declaration of Helsinki / Helsinki Declaration

Patterns are NOT designed to capture: - General ethical considerations or ethical dilemmas in study content - Mentions of “ethics” in theoretical or philosophical contexts - Author approval of a manuscript (e.g. “all authors approved the final version”) - Ethical behaviour as a measured variable (e.g. “ethical decision-making”) - URLs containing “ethics” in path components

Live data collection is detected by the internal helper .detect_live_data(), which searches for sentences indicating that data were collected directly from human or animal participants. Papers without any live-data signal are not flagged as missing ethics approval. The helper uses conservative patterns to avoid flagging secondary data analyses, computational experiments, or economics papers that analyse existing survey data. See .detect_live_data() for the full list of patterns and intentional exclusions.

A paper that states that no human or animal subjects took part (“no human subjects were involved”, “did not involve human participants”, or people taking part “not as subjects”) is not expected to have an ethics statement, whatever participant phrase it also has (see .detect_no_participants()). A negation near a participant phrase alone (“No participants were excluded”) does not count: it reports a study with participants.

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Power Analysis Check works

This module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. If specified by the user, it also uses a large language model (LLM) to extract information reported in power analyses, including the statistical test, sample size, alpha level, desired level of power, and magnitude and type of effect size.

The Power Analysis Check module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. Without the use of an LLM, the module uses regular expressions to classify the power analysis as a-priori, sensitivity or post-hoc. With the use of an LLM, it checks if the power analysis is reported with all required information.

The regular expressions can miss power analyses, or fail to classify them correctly. The type of power analysis is often difficult to classify, which can easily be solved by explicitly specifying the type of power analysis as ‘a-priori’, ‘sensitivity’, or ‘post-hoc’. Note that ‘post-hoc’ or ‘observed’ power is rarely useful. The LLM can fail to identify information in the paper, and will not have access to information in paragraphs in the paper other than those that contain the word ‘power’. This package was validated by the Metacheck team on articles in Psychological Science.

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine, Daniel Lakens and Cristian Mesquida

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 128 papers with 246 instances of power statements, 203 were correctly detected (true positives), 22 were missed (false negatives) and 21 were incorrectly detected (false positives). Overall, among all instances flagged as power statements, 90.6% were correct (positive predictive value).

How Preregistration Check works

Retrieve information from preregistrations in a standardised way, and make them easier to check.

The Preregistration Check module identifies preregistrations on the OSF and AsPredicted based on links in the manuscript, retrieves the preregistration text, and organizes the information into a template. The module retrieves text from the OSF with its API, and from AsPredicted with ResearchBox’s API when a ResearchBox key is set (see rbox_token()), or else from the preregistration’s web page. The information in the preregistration is returned. An AsPredicted link that could not be read is named in the report, with the reason.

The module can’t extract information from non-structured preregistration templates (i.e., where the preregistration is uploaded in a single text field) and it can’t retrieve information in preregistrations that are stored as text documents on the OSF.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download information from other preregistration sites, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Marginal Significance works

List all sentences that describe an effect as ‘marginally significant’.

The marginal module searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The list of terms is a subset of those listed in a blog post by Matthew Hankins. The module returns all sentences that match terms describing ‘marginally significant’ results.

Some of the terms identified might not be problematic in some contexts, and there are ways to describe ‘marginal significance’ that are not detected by the module.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 51 papers with 87 statements, this module correctly identified 38 statements (true positives) and incorrectly flagged 22 statements (false positives). It failed to detect 27 statements. Thus, among all statements flagged by the module, 63% were genuine cases (positive predictive value). However, the module missed 42% of all true statements (false negative rate).

How StatCheck works

Check consistency of p-values and test statistics

The Statcheck module runs Statcheck. Statcheck searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern, and identifies APA reported statistical tests. More information on the package can be found at https://github.com/cran/statcheck. The module only returns Statcheck results for t-tests and F-tests, as these are the only tests which have been validated, see https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/.

Statcheck was developed by Michèle Nuijten and Sascha Epskamp.

Statcheck considers p = 0.000 an error, as you should report p < 0.001. Furthermore, p < 0.03 is an error if the p-value was 0.031, and one should simply report exact p-values (p = 0.031). Statcheck might miss one-sided tests, and falsely assume the p-value is incorrect. For more information, see StatCheck.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 685 tests with 34 instances of inconsistent reporting, Statcheck correctly detected 34 of them, and incorrectly identified 26. Therefore 0% of true instances were missed, and 43% of detections were false positives. See https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/ for more details of the validation.

How Exact P-Values works

List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.) or reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000).

This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001.

A p-value that is not the result of a test is not flagged: a table note (“* p < .05, ** p < .01”), a figure legend (“Asterisks indicate significant differences (p < .05)”, “Values in bold are significant at p < .05”) or a stated threshold (“p < .05 was considered significant”, “thresholded at p < .001”). GROBID often puts such notes into the running text, so each p-value is judged by the words in its own clause (the text up to a “;” or a full stop), and never left out when a test statistic belongs to it (“F(1, 7) = 8.03, # p < .05”). The column not_a_test of the table says why a p-value was left out (“marker”, “threshold” or “legend”). Notes in other forms, such as a marker after the p-value (“p < .05 (*)“), are still flagged.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (“decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table’s footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above).

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 225 papers containing 405 instances of non-exact p-values, the module correctly detected 269 cases (true positives) and incorrectly identified 78 (false positives). It missed 136 instances of imprecisely reported p-values (false negatives) and correctly identified 4557 cases of precisely reported p-values (true negative). Additionally, 78% of positive detections were correct (positive predictive value).

How Non-Significant P Value Check works

This module checks for imprecisely reported p values. If p > .05 is detected, it warns for misinterpretations.

The nonsignificant p-value check searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The module identifies all p-values in a manuscript and selects those that are not reported to be smaller than or equal to 0.05. It returns all sentences containing non-significant p-values.

In the future, the Metacheck team aims to incorporate a machine learning classifier to only return sentences likely to contain misinterpretations. If you want to help to improve the module, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 194 papers with 1602 instances of non-significant p-values, this module correctly detected 1486 of them, and incorrectly identified 153. Additionally, 91% of detections were true instances (positive predictive value). That is, when this module flags non-significant p-values in a paper, it correctly identifies an issue 91% of the time.

How Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests works

The Effect Size module checks if effect sizes are correctly reported in t-tests and F-tests.

The Effect Size check searches for regular expressions that match typical ways in which effect sizes are reported. It subsequently checks different ways in which Cohen’s d, g, ηp2, and ωp2 can be computed against the reported value. If effects are missing, or might be incorrect, you the module provides a warning. The module was validated on APA reported statistical tests, and might miss effect sizes that were reported in other reporting styles. It was validated by the Metacheck team on papers published in Psychological Science.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 161 papers with 1469 tests, this module correctly detected 1106 reported effect sizes (true positives) and correctly identified 295 cases where no effect size was present (true negatives). However, it missed 23 that were reported (false negatives), and incorrectly identified 45 effect sizes when none were reported (false positives). Among all instances detected by the module, 96% were true cases (positive predictive value). In a validation against 221 reported Cohen’s d effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 218 cases (99%). In a validation against 485 partial eta-squared effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 480 (99%)

How Codebook Check works

This module checks whether the data columns in a repository are documented in a codebook or README. It locates codebook/readme files, extracts the variable definitions they contain, matches those definitions against the data columns extracted by data_check, and reports documentation coverage: how many data columns are documented, and which documented variables are never used.

The Codebook Check module consumes the columns and file classification produced by data_check (and, transitively, repo_check). Files classified as codebook or readme are parsed with parse_codebook(), which reads structured tables (CSV/TSV/Excel with a variable-name column and a label column), embedded labels in haven files (SPSS/Stata/SAS), and plain text from rich-text formats (docx/pdf/rtf/odt). Embedded haven labels from data files are also harvested directly.

Each data column is then matched against the parsed variable definitions with match_column_labels(), using normalised-name matching with experiment-group scoping, haven-label priority, and rule-based label-equivalence merging.

Beyond the variable label, the module harvests the DDI-style per-variable properties a source supplies: the value labels / code list (the 1=“Strongly disagree”…5=“Strongly agree” mapping — from SPSS/Stata value labels and from a codebook “values”/“coding” column), the missing-value scheme (which codes denote missingness, from haven declared missings and labels that read as “refused”/“n/a”), and question text and columns when present. These are carried onto the matched data columns and exported into the Psych-DS variableMeasured (as a schema.org code list plus namespaced metacheck: fields).

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE). When llm_use(TRUE), three optional LLM tiers run: parsing unstructured codebook text that the rules could not handle, fuzzy-matching still-unlabelled columns to still-unmatched codebook variables, and merging conflicting label definitions into a single canonical label.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the codebook_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Repository Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories.

The Repository Check module lists files on the OSF, GitHub, ResearchBox, DSpace (PsychArchives and other legacy- and DSpace 7-based installations), Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, Mendeley Data, DataONE (Arctic Data Center, KNB, and other member nodes), and LDbase based on links in the manuscript.

Listing a repository’s files never requires an API key, but some hosts answer faster or more completely with one: OSF allows 100 requests/hour unauthenticated versus 10,000/day with a token (see [osf_pat()]), and Dryad enforces a strict per-IP daily quota on repeated listing (see cache below). Dryad is a special case beyond rate limits: listing a Dryad dataset’s files works without a key, but actually downloading file CONTENTS from Dryad fails with HTTP 401 unless a key is set, even for a fully public dataset (see [dryad_pat()] or [dryad_auth()]). Since this module only lists files and never downloads their contents itself, that limitation applies to data_check and code_check (which do download content), not here – see their own documentation.

When a linked OSF page is a registration, its registered_from project (the one it was registered from, which the manuscript itself may never link directly) is also checked: if that project is public its files are listed under its own URL, and if it is closed or otherwise inaccessible the report flags it explicitly, since some registrations only describe their content rather than mirroring it.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download files from additional data repositories reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the repo_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Code Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories checked by repo_check about code files (R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, MATLAB).

The Code Check module checks R (also R Markdown and Quarto), Python (also Jupyter notebooks), SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB files, using regular expressions to check the code; JASP files are listed but not read. The language of a Quarto document or a notebook is read from the file itself (its engine or kernel), not from its extension. The regular expression search will detect the number of comments, the lines at which libraries/imports are loaded, attempts to detect absolute paths to files, setwd() and install.packages() calls, and lists files that are loaded, and checks if these files are in the repository; R code is also parsed. The module will return suggestions to improve the code if there are no comments, if libraries/imports are loaded in lines further than 4 lines apart, if files that are loaded are not in the repository, if absolute file paths, setwd() or install.packages() are found, and if R code cannot be parsed.

The regular expressions can miss information in code files, or falsely detect parts of the code as a fixed file path. Libraries/imports might be loaded in one block, even if there are more than 3 intermittent lines. The module was tried out internally on papers published in Psychological Science, but has not been formally validated. There might be valid reasons why some loaded files can’t be shared, but the module can’t evaluate these reasons, and always gives a warning.

The module also checks whether the repository pins the R/package versions the analysis actually depended on: an renv.lock file (parsed for the R version and every locked package + its version/source), a sessionInfo()/sessioninfo::session_info() text dump (matched by filename — sessionInfo.txt/session_info.txt and similar, or embedded in a README), or a groundhog::groundhog.library()/checkpoint::checkpoint() date-pin call in the code (a bare library(groundhog)/library(checkpoint) does not count — the pinning call itself must be present). When none of these is found, the report flags it as a reproducibility gap: package versions may drift between when the analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt.

If you want to extend the package to perform additional checks on code files, or make the checks work on other types of code files, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

Checking code requires downloading its file contents. For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this never succeeds unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (listing the repository’s files does not need one). Without a key, every Dryad-hosted code file is listed but unchecked, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures recorded in the manifest.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Raphael Merz

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the code_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Data Check works

This module classifies the files in a repository into semantic types (data, codebook, code, software, output, supplemental, readme, asset, other) and, for tabular data files, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

The Data Check module consumes the file list produced by repo_check (or any files added via local_path). Each file is classified with rule-based heuristics layered over metacheck’s file_category() and file_types: file names matching README / codebook patterns win first, then an extension crosswalk, then format-locked extension overrides. For every file classified as tabular data that is available locally, the module reads the file head, describes each column with data_col_facets() and computes summary statistics for numeric columns. Every sheet of a spreadsheet that holds a table is read: a file with several such sheets has its columns under source_file = "file.xlsx [sheet]", and the sheet column names the sheet of any spreadsheet with several sheets; a sheet of notes or a codebook is treated as documentation when the file has another table. Following DDI, a column is described by orthogonal facets rather than a single type: representation (numeric/text/datetime/code — how it is stored), measurement_level (Stevens: nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio), concept (what it measures: reaction_time/age/gender/likert/id/…), role (identifier/measure/condition/timestamp), unit, and a quality state (ok/empty/constant). Concepts are detected by name+value rules (the demographic concepts via data_check_demographic()); when llm_use(TRUE) the model fills concepts and measurement levels the rules left blank. Qualtrics survey exports are recognised (data_check_is_qualtrics()): their extra header rows are stripped so columns type correctly, and the reserved response-metadata columns (StartDate, Duration, Finished, …) are tagged.

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE): columns the rules cannot resolve (ambiguous 3–20-unique integers, ambiguous character columns) fall back to continuous / text respectively. When llm_use(TRUE), ambiguous columns and unresolved file types (other) are sent to llm() for optional refinement, and every file is assigned a study group (ex1, pilot2, shared, …) so that multi-study repositories can be recognised (used by psychds_check). Without an LLM the study group is left NA (unknown).

Column extraction requires files to be readable from disk. Files fetched by repo_check from OSF/GitHub/etc. without a local copy (file_location is NA) are classified but not column-extracted; pass local_path to point at a downloaded copy of the repository.

For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this means column extraction never happens unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (dataset listing and metadata do not need one). Without a key, every Dryad file stays classified but un-downloaded, column_n is 0, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures. A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

Every downloaded text file the authors wrote (code, settings, survey definitions such as Qualtrics .qsf files, documentation, outputs) is searched for keys: API keys, access tokens and private keys, which let anyone who downloads the file use a paid service at the authors’ cost. Of a tabular data file only the column names and first 3 rows of the table as read are searched: its values come from participants, but a key the authors set for a whole survey (as embedded data in a Qualtrics survey flow) is exported in every response. The search uses the rules of the secret scanner betterleaks (https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks, MIT licence) of high and medium confidence. A key found turns the traffic light red; the report and the keys table give its file, line and type, and only its beginning. Other files over 25 MB and binary files are not searched. A key is never tested with its provider. Every module’s result has any whole key replaced by “keyremoved” (see module_run()).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Levi Baruch

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

The Retrieving Effectively from Memory (REM) model (Shiffrin & Stevyers, 1997) is an extremely influential model of old-new recognition memory based on Bayesian reasoning principles that provides a comprehensive account of diverse memory phenomena. However, a limitation of extant versions of the model is that it does not provide accounts of recognition memory at the level of individual items based on their precise positions in multidimensional similarity space and their possession of item-specific distinctive features. Instead, it assumes a geometric probability distribution for generating hypothetical features and relies on computer simulation to generate predictions of patterns of results for large classes of items and experimental manipulations. Here we move in the direction of filling that gap by proposing a REM-like model in which individual items are represented in one-to-one correspondence as points in multidimensional similarity (MDS) spaces and in which information regarding distinctive features possessed by individual objects is also provided. Rather than using the geometric-probability distribution assumed by Shiffrin and Steyvers, this "MDS-REM" model uses continuous probability density functions defined over the continuous-dimension MDS spaces. The model is tested using data sets from three previously reported perceptual old-new recognition studies and provides reasonably accurate predictions of performance at the level of individual items or categories, including accounts of how both false-alarm and hit rates are influenced by detailed similarity relations among items and their possession of item-specific distinctive features.

[div-01]

A central topic addressed in the cognitive-psychology of episodic memory is how observers make recognition judgments of whether items are "old" (previously experienced) or "new". Among the major computational models of old-new recognition memory are members of the class of "global-familiarity" models (Gillund & Shiffrin, 1984; Hintzman, 1988; Kahana & Sekuler, 2002; Murdock, 1982; Nosofsky, 1988 Nosofsky, , 1991;; Osth, Zhang, & Williams, 2025; Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997; for reviews, see Clark & Gronlund, 1996; Osth & Dennis, 2024). According to this class of models, presentation of a test item leads to a global-activation of the contents of memory based on how similar the test item is to the underlying memory representations. The greater the global activation, the more familiar the item seems, and the greater is the probability that the observer judges the item to be old. Although prominent models have also been proposed that posit that there are multiple processes underlying old-new recognition (e.g., Malmberg, Holden, & Shiffrin, 2004; Wixted, 2007; Yonelinas, 2002), the focus in this article is on the single-process global-familiarity class.

Our specific focus in this article is on a member of the class of global-familiarity models proposed by Shiffrin and Steyvers (1997) known as REM (Retrieving Effectively from Memory).

We describe the detailed computational ideas in REM below. The general idea, however, is that by making a global comparison of a test item to the contents of memory, the memory system computes the likelihood that the test item is "old" and the likelihood that the test item is "new" and forms a ratio of these likelihoods. If the likelihood ratio exceeds a criterion value -which has an ideal-observer value equal to 1, reflecting an equal likelihood that the item is old or new -then the system responds "old", else the system responds "new".

The original version of REM as well as significant extensions of the model (Cox & Shiffrin, 2017; Criss, 2006; Criss, Malmberg, & Shiffrin, 2011; Mohamed, Meyer-Grant, & Shiffrin, 2026) have proven successful at accounting for an enormous collection of fundamental results from the old-new recognition literature, including the list-length effect, the null liststrength effect, the mirror effect, the shape of ROC curves, word-frequency effects, effects of presentation time and signal-to-respond methods, memory for pictures versus words, effects of "oldness" vs. "newness" judgments in wide varieties of forced-choice recognition tasks, and numerous other fundamental results. This coverage is impressive when one considers that many of these results were challenging for previous models to explain (Glanzer & Adams, 1990; Ratcliff, Sheu, & Gronlund, 1992; Shiffrin, Ratcliff, & Clark, 1990).

However, a limitation of extant versions of the model is they are not designed to predict the probability with which observers recognize individual items as being old or new based on the items' precise locations in a multidimensional similarity space. The reason is that extant versions of REM do not identify specific multidimensional representations corresponding to specific items tested in experiments. Instead, applications of the model use simulation techniques in which features of hypothetical items are generated by using a geometric-probability distribution. This approach is used for representing general "classes" of items, such as low-frequency or highfrequency words and pictures, but the modeling approach does not develop individualized representations corresponding in one-to-one fashion to the individual items themselves. This is an obvious downside when one considers that the prediction of individual-item identification and old-new recognition based on the positions of items in multidimensional similarity space has been a classic goal in past tests of cognitive-process models of memory (e.g., Nosofsky, 1988 Nosofsky, , 1991 Nosofsky, , 1992;; Shepard, 1957 Shepard, , 1958)). Furthermore, this goal is an emerging direction in modern computational modeling work aimed at predicting individual-item recognition for items drawn from high-dimensional, real-world perceptual and semantic domains (e.g., Chang, Johns, & Brainerd, 2025; Meagher & Nosofsky, 2023; Nosofsky, Ehinger, & Osth, 2025; Osth, Zhang, & Williams, 2026; Reid & Jamieson, 2023). Much of this modern computational modeling work is motivated by the recent literature on "memorability" that seeks to understand why certain realworld individual items are recognized with high accuracy and others are more easily forgotten (Bainbridge, 2019; Kramer, Hebart, et al., 2023). We discuss this literature in more detail in our General Discussion.

Thus, the central purpose of the present work was to move in the direction of adapting REM to allow it to make such individual-item predictions. Before proceeding, we should note that this goal was pursued long ago by Mark Steyvers in his 2000 Ph.D. dissertation in the domain of word recognition (Steyvers, 2000). Using a large database of free association norms, Steyvers located individual words in word-association spaces and combined these representations with REM to predict a variety of qualitative effects in word-recognition experiments. However, although his approach yielded predictions of individual-word hit and false-alarm rates that improved upon models that represent words with arbitrary features, he characterized the achieved correlations as "moderate". In the present work, we propose a REMlike model intended to capture results at the level of individual items in domains of perceptual old-new recognition rather than word recognition and use alternative methods for locating the items in multidimensional similarity spaces.

At the outset, we need to emphasize that the original version of REM was developed in the form of an ideal-observer model derived from a Bayesian likelihood-ratio framework. To derive the model, Shiffrin and Steyvers (1997) assumed a probabilistic world in which the features that composed old study items and new lures were generated from an identical geometric-probability distribution. The study items were presumed to be stored in noisy fashion in memory. Given their specific assumptions, Shiffrin and Steyvers developed precise idealobserver equations for computing the likelihoods that test items were old or new (for details, see Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997, pp. 147, 163) and the model would respond that the test item was "old" if the computed likelihood-ratio exceeded a criterion (often set to an optimal value of 1).

As explained above, however, any simulated item that was stored in memory was intended to serve only as a representative from a general class of items -the simulated memory representation did not correspond to any specific item tested in the behavioral experiments.

In the present work, we retain core ideas motivated by original REM but no longer operate in the probabilistic world defined by the geometric probability distribution that was assumed by Shiffrin and Steyvers. Instead, because our goal will be to develop a REM-like model capable of predicting old-new recognition probabilities for individual items lying in continuous-dimension similarity spaces, we will make use of continuous probability functions defined in those spaces. Although the model will retain many of the core conceptual ideas from original REM, we make no claims that the version that we develop and test is an ideal-observer model.

Our REM-like alternative differs from original REM in another important way. In the original REM model, the researchers simulated probabilistic memory representations for study items that differed from one simulation to the next and then applied a deterministic decision rule for making old-new recognition judgments in any given simulation. The predictions of old-new judgments were probabilistic because of noisy storage of the study items across the multiple simulations. This use of simulation techniques made quantitative parameter-estimation difficult, so the researchers often reported parameter settings that yielded good qualitative accounts of the overall patterns of results without necessarily achieving optimal quantitative fits. By comparison, here we will be interested in using our REM-like model for generating precise quantitative predictions at the level of individual items, which will require challenging and computationally expensive parameter searches. To make this goal more tractable, we will assume for simplicity that the observer stores error-free versions of the study items in memory and we will place the "noise" in observers' judgments within a probabilistic decision rule rather than using a deterministic one. An advantage of implementing the model in this manner is that it can be expressed in analytic form without the need for use of computer simulation.

Integrating Individual-Item MDS Representations and Distinctive-Feature Information Within the MDS-REM Model

Our proposed REM-like model borrows ideas from another global-familiarity model of old-new recognition, namely the hybrid-similarity generalized context model (GCM) of Nosofsky and Zaki (2003). That model has proven successful at predicting varieties of old-new recognition at the level of individual items, including recent applications in high-dimensional real-world domains (Meagher & Nosofsky, 2023; Nosofsky, Ehinger, & Osth, 2025). Therefore, before transitioning to our proposed adaptation of REM, we first briefly describe the gist of the hybrid-similarity GCM and an example experiment to which it has been applied. This experiment will also serve as our first testing ground for our proposed adapted version of REM.

A core idea in the hybrid-similarity GCM is to use multidimensional-scaling (MDS) techniques to embed objects in continuous multidimensional similarity spaces (Lee, 2001; Shepard, 1958 Shepard, , 1980)). These same MDS representations will be used in our proposed adaptation of REM; thus, for ease of description, we will term our proposed adaptation the MDS-REM model. Beyond the use of the continuous-dimension MDS representation, however, the hybridsimilarity GCM also incorporates an independent set of ratings that measure the presence of "distinctive features" possessed by the objects. As explained below, the distinctive features seem intuitively to "stand outside" of the derived continuous MDS spaces. Extensive past research has demonstrated the fundamental importance of item distinctiveness in mediating old-new recognition and these distinctiveness ratings have played a fundamental role in allowing the hybrid-similarity GCM to account quantitatively for varieties of old-new recognition performance. The MDS-REM model will make use of these distinctive-feature ratings as well.

Although the hybrid-similarity GCM and MDS-REM model both make use of the same MDS and distinctive-feature information in computing a global-familiarity signal across all stored memory traces, we will see some potentially important conceptual differences between the models in how they make use of the information. Our focus here will be on the newly proposed MDS-REM model, but we provide a fuller discussion of the relation between the models in our General Discussion.

In a recent test of the hybrid-similarity GCM, Meagher and Nosofsky (2023) reported an experiment in which observers learned to classify a set of 180 rock-image stimuli into three geologically-defined superordinate categories (igneous, metamorphic and sedimentary). (There were 6 training items sampled from each of 10 subtype categories composing each of the 3 superordinate categories, for a total of 180 training items.) Following the training phase, observers engaged in a classification transfer-test phase involving the original 180 training items and 360 novel transfer stimuli. In addition, during the transfer test, observers made recognition judgments of whether each of the 540 individual items was old or new. In this article we focus on only the old-new recognition data. Importantly, a subset of the novel transfer items had a special status of being "high-similarity neighbors" (HSNs): Meagher and Nosofsky (2023) used photoshopping techniques to construct a set of HSN lures that were highly similar to individual target items from the old training set (for illustrative examples, see Meagher & Nosofsky, 2023, Figure 1). The expectation was that false-alarm rates for the HSN lures would be relatively high in magnitude.

In previous work, Nosofsky et al. (2018 Nosofsky et al. ( , 2020) ) and Meagher and Nosofsky (2023) had collected extensive similarity scaling data and conducted MDS analyses of the similarity data to embed the 540 rock images in a multidimensional similarity space. Based on a combination of overall fit and interpretability of the derived dimensions, they settled on use of an 8-dimensional MDS solution for representing the individual images in the continuous-dimension space. The dimensions of the space correlated strongly with attribute ratings (provided by independent groups of subjects) of lightness/darkness, average grain size, smoothness/roughness, shininess, chromaticity, organization, red/green hue, and shape-related components. However, many of the rock images also had highly idiosyncratic distinctive features that seemed to go "outside" this continuous-dimension space. For example, obsidian is a smooth, shiny, dark black glassy rock; however, one of the obsidian samples had a series of prominent bright red stripes across its surface that seemed to make it "stand out" from other rock images in the set. Other examples include rocks with prominent embedded crystals or a rock with a prominent fossil embedded in it. As a proxy for the existence of such distinctive features, a separate group of participants provided ratings of the extent to which each rock image possessed a highly distinctive feature not present in other items in the set. (For examples of rock images that received high vs. low distinctive-feature ratings, see Fig. 12 of Meagher & Nosofsky, 2023.) Although these ratings provide partial information about presence of distinctive features, a limitation is that the method does not identify the actual specific distinctive features that are present in each item. This limitation will require us to use certain approximations when implementing the MDS-REM model. The MDS solution for the rock images as well as the mean distinctive feature ratings are available at https://osf.io/cvwu9/.

Before presenting the MDS-REM equations, we highlight a key conceptual issue involving the prediction of hit and false-alarm rates in old-new recognition that needs to be addressed by MDS-REM (and all members of the class of global-familiarity models). In general, global-familiarity models predict higher probabilities of false alarms when lures are highly similar to the study items than when they have low similarity. In such cases, summed interitem similarity (i.e., global-familiarity) will be high, so observers will have a higher probability of false-alarming to such lures. The picture is not so clear regarding the prediction of hit rates for old targets. On the one hand, if an old target is embedded in a dense region of the similarity space (i.e., if it is similar to many other old study items), then many traditional global-familiarity models (e.g., Gillund & Shiffrin, 1984; Hintzman, 1988; Nosofsky, 1991) would predict that it too would tend to have high summed interitem similarity, so presumably would generate a relatively high-magnitude familiarity signal. Using this line of reasoning, the expectation would be that targets located in dense regions of the similarity space should have relatively high hit rates.

Empirical evidence suggests, however, that exactly the opposite is true: it is often the case that highly distinctive old targets that lie in isolated, sparse regions of the similarity space have the highest hit rates. For example, as brought out by Valentine and Ferrara (1991) and Busey and Tunnicluff (1999), faces with highly distinctive scars that lie in sparse regions of multidimensional similarity space often have higher hit rates than do more typical faces without such distinctive features. In the hybrid-similarity GCM (Nosofsky & Zaki, 2003), the proposed explanation for this pattern of results is that targets with highly distinctive features have higher self-similarity to their own representations than do targets without such features. This idea is directly motivated by Tversky's (1977) feature-contrast model of similarity, which predicts that the addition of salient features to an object will boost its self-similarity. If the boosted selfsimilarity is sufficiently high, then overall global summed similarity (which is a combination of self-similarity and summed interitem similarity) will also be very high, and observers will display high hit rates for items with highly distinctive features. The hybrid-similarity GCM has provided reasonably good accounts of patterns of old-new recognition involving items with distinctive features in its previous tests (Azarov & Nosofsky, in press; Knapp, Nosofsky, & Busey, 2006; Meagher & Nosofsky, 2023; Nosofsky, Ehinger, & Osth, 2025; Nosofsky & Zaki, 2003), whereas the model fails to account for the data if the role of the distinctive features is not incorporated in its machinery. As we will see, the version of MDS-REM that we propose has an alternative conceptual explanation for the reason why items with highly distinctive features often have high hit rates. Nevertheless, incorporating information about the presence of the distinctive features will be critical to its operation as well. We return to this crucial issue after providing our formal statement of our modified REM-like model.

Formal Statement of MDS-REM Shiffrin and Steyvers's (1997) original REM model assumes that individual items presented on a study list are represented as individual traces in memory; however, due to noise in encoding, some features either are not stored or are stored incorrectly. Our newly proposed MDS-REM also assumes that each study item is represented as an individual memory trace; however, in our adapted version of the model, we assume for simplicity that all the complete memory traces are stored and that they are stored in an error-free manner. In our situation, the study and test items are assumed to reside in a continuous multidimensional space with M dimensions. The value of each item i on each dimension m is given by its coordinate value on dimension m (xim) in the MDS solution derived for the objects.

The original REM assumed that each item on a study list of size n has been presented one time on the study list and we adopt this simplifying assumption as well. Each study item gives rise to an individualized memory trace. Following Shiffrin and Steyvers (1997), the resulting set of n memory traces constitutes the "data" (D) and each individual memory trace is denoted by Dj. Because of our assumption of error-free storage, the values of each Dj along its M MDS dimensions are simply the coordinates of item j in the MDS solution. Recall that the test items and memory traces are also presumed to possess distinctive features that go outside the continuous MDS solution, and these will be incorporated in the model's machinery as well (see below).

Following Shiffrin and Steyvers (1997), conditioned upon presentation of some test item i, the system computes: 1) the probability that the test item is "old" (O) given the complete collection of memory-trace data (D), P(O|D); and 2) the probability that the test item is "new" (N) given the complete collection of memory-trace data, P(N|D). It then forms the likelihood ratio (LR) of these computations:

Using Bayes Theorem, and following the assumptions, derivations and notation from Shiffrin and Steyvers (1997, p. 163), this Equation-1 likelihood-ratio is given by

In Equation 2, Sj is the notation for what Shiffrin and Steyvers refer to as a "same image", and use of this notation means that the system is supposing that memory-trace j (Dj) was the memory trace produced by the current test probe i during the study phase. The value P(Dj| Sj) is the probability that the memory-trace Dj would have been produced by test-probe i. Conceptually, in each numerator of the terms in Equation 2, the system is going one-by-one through each of the n memory traces and computing the probability that each memory trace Dj would have been produced by the current test-probe i. Note that, given our assumptions, if test probe i is an old target item, in only one of these n cases is memory trace j the actual memory trace that was produced by test item i. If test probe i is a novel lure, then in none of these cases were the memory traces j produced by test probe i. Whereas the numerator in the terms of Equation 2gives the probability that each memory trace Dj would have been produced by test probe i during the study phase, the denominator of each term gives the probability that the memory trace would have been produced by a new-item-generation process (denoted Nj), which we describe below.

We return to these P(Dj| Nj) terms in the denominators later in our presentation.

The immediate question now is how to compute the values of P(Dj|Sj) in the numerators of Equation 2. With regard to the continuous MDS coordinates that compose the traces, our proposal is that the system assumes that each memory trace is a multivariate normal distortion of whatever test probe i created it, with the mean of the multivariate normal being the coordinates of test probe i itself. For simplicity, we assume that each dimension of the multivariate normal has the same standard deviation σs and that there is zero correlation between any pair of dimensions. In the case in which the test probe i really does correspond to a specific memory trace j, the probe and memory trace will have identical values of the distinctive features (given our assumption of error-free storage), so the distinctive-feature component will not "subtract" from the probability density that memory trace j would be produced by test probe i. In short, in the case in which test probe i was the actual study item that produced memory-trace j, the memory system's computation of the probability-density of memory trace j given test-probe i would be given by

Note that in this particular case in which test-probe i really did produce memory-trace j, the values xim = xjm across all M dimensions, so P(Dj|Sj) is simply equal to

Suppose instead that test probe i was not the study item that had produced memory-trace j. [Assume further that we are not dealing with the special case described earlier in which the test probe is a high-similarity neighbor (HSN) of the study item that produced memory-trace j.]

Within the continuous MDS space, the probability-density P(Dj|Sj) is computed in the same manner as in Equation 3a, except now the values xim and xjm will be mismatching across the M dimensions, yielding a lower probability density that memory-trace j was produced by test probe i. In addition, the test probe and the memory trace are now very unlikely to share the same distinctive features; we will assume for simplicity that their distinctive features do in fact differ from one another. This mismatch on the distinctive features will further reduce the memory system's computation of P(Dj|Sj).

In the present paradigm, we do not know the actual identity of the distinctive features of each item, but the ratings of feature distinctiveness provided by the independent group of participants allows us to approximate the amount of reduction that is involved. Let δi ' denote the mean distinctive feature rating that participants in the rating study provided to test probe i, and let δj ' denote the mean distinctive feature rating that participants in the rating study provided to item j. Because the absolute magnitudes of the scale of distinctive feature ratings are arbitrary, we make allowance for a monotonic, nonlinear transformation of the raw mean ratings onto a psychological distinctiveness scale (for details, see Appendix A), producing transformed distinctive-feature ratings δi and δj. Then, for this case in which test probe i did not actually produce memory-trace j, the probability density of memory trace j given test probe i is given by where αT and αM are freely estimated scaling parameters that weight the importance of the distinctive features of the test probes and memory traces respectively.

(The parameter values αT and αM do not depend on which specific items serve as test probes versus memory traces; they are fixed scaling constants.) Intuitively, for example, to the extent that test probe i has a highly distinctive feature not shared by memory trace j, the probability density that test probe i might have produced memory-trace j is reduced. Likewise, if memory trace j includes a highly distinctive feature not shared by test probe i, then the probability density that probe i produced trace j is also reduced. We make allowance for separate values of αT and αM because there may be differential, asymmetric influences of distinctive features of test probes and memory traces on the memory system's computations of the probability densities. Note that the same Equation 4holds both for test probes that were study items but not ones that produced a particular memory-trace j and for standard lures presented during the test phase. For reasons already explained above, the values of P(Dj|Sj) yielded by such test probes will be considerably lower than the one yielded for a test probe that actually did produce memory-trace j.

Finally, for the present paradigm, a special case of P(Dj|Sj) to consider is one which the test probe is an HSN lure. Consider in particular the case in which a specific memory-trace j was produced by the study item that is the "parent" of the HSN lure. Unlike for standard lures, in this case the distinctive features of the HSN lure are likely to be quite similar to the distinctive features of this special-case memory trace (because they were both produced by the same parent). Thus, in this special case, the memory system would reduce the probability density P(Dj|Sj) to a much smaller degree than for standard lures.

To capture this behavior of the memory system, the model assumes that, for the special case in which an HSN lure is being compared to the memory trace produced by its parent, the probability density with which the HSN lure would produce the parent-generated memory trace is given by where v is a fixed freely estimated scaling parameter that reduces the magnitude of the mismatch between the distinctive features of the HSN lure and its parent-generated memory trace.

1 For all other comparisons involving HSN lures, the previous Equation 4 applies for computing P(Dj|Sj).

For the reasons explained above, our expectation is that the estimate of v will be less than one.

The next step in the modeling is to set values for the P(Dj|Nj) probability densities that appear in the denominators of the individual-trace likelihood-ratio terms in Equation 2.

Conceptually, these values are providing estimates that each memory trace j would have been produced by some new-item-generation process. Recall that Shiffrin and Steyvers (1997) assumed that the same geometric probability distribution produced the features of old and new test probes, which allowed them to develop their ideal-observer model. By contrast, the specification of a new-item-generation process in the present continuous-dimension domain is more open-ended. We formulated two candidate versions of our proposed MDS-REM model for this purpose, although a wide variety of other candidates are possible. In the first, we imagined that the memory system assumes that all items are being randomly sampled from a single Mdimensional multivariate normal distribution with mean on each dimension m (μm) equal to the mean of all the study items on each dimension m. For simplicity, we assumed a constant standard deviation σN on each of the dimensions of this multivariate normal and zero correlation between all pairs of dimensions. To provide the model with some flexibility, we allowed the value of σN to be a free parameter (rather than computing it from the study items). In addition, we needed to make provision for the probability that the new-item generation process would generate whatever distinctive feature might be possessed by memory-trace j. The overall probability density that the new-item generation process would produce memory-trace j was therefore given by where, as before, the xjm are the values of item j on each dimension m of the MDS space; μm is the dimension-m mean of the multivariate normal that generates new items in the space (assumed here to be the mean computed across all study items); and δj is the (transformed) distinctivefeature rating for item j.

As discussed above, the multivariate-normal standard deviation σN is allowed to be a free parameter. Finally, the value αN is a freely estimated scaling parameter that influences the magnitude of the reduction of P(Dj|Nj) that results from the distinctive feature possessed by memory-trace j. Conceptually, Equation 6 formalizes two ideas: First, the probability density P(Dj|Nj) will tend to be small if memory-trace j lies in an isolated region of the space, because it is less likely for the new-item generation process to generate items in isolated regions. Second, the probability density P(Dj|Nj) will tend to be small if memory-trace j possesses a highly distinctive feature, because it is less likely for the new-item generation process to generate an item with some specific highly distinctive feature.

We have now completed the presentation of the steps required for computing all the P(Dj|Sj) and P(Dj|Nj) values in the likelihood-ratio Equation 2. The final step is to use the computed likelihood-ratio (LR) value for generating a predicted probability that the test probe is judged to be old. This probability is assumed to be given by where k is a criterion parameter; and γ is a freely estimated response-scaling parameter (e.g., Meagher & Nosofsky, 2023).

The system tends to respond "old" when LR γ exceeds k and tends to respond "new" otherwise.

As noted above, we also formulated a second version of the MDS-REM model that assumed an alternative new-item generation process. In brief, rather than assuming that new items were generated by sampling from a single multivariate normal, the second version integrated across the positions of the individual study items to estimate the probability that a new memory trace would be randomly generated in its respective location of the MDS space. The fits of this second version were extremely similar to those of the first, so we present the detailed formulation of the second version in Appendix B.

Before turning to the sections of our article in which we show fits of the proposed MDS-REM model to data, it is useful to flesh out the conceptual underpinnings of the model and the types of predictions we expect it will make. First, in general, the model will of course tend to predict that hit rates to old items will be higher than false-alarm rates to new items. In the case of an old test probe, there will be a perfect match to a single memory trace, and here the value of P(Dj|Sj) will reach its maximum, leading to a large-magnitude LR value (see Equations 2 and 3b).

Second, lures that are highly similar to numerous memory traces will have high false-alarm rates.

In this case, even though such lures will not provide a perfect match to any given memory trace, many of the P(Dj|Sj) will be reasonably high, again leading to a relatively large-magnitude LR value (see Equations 2, 4, and 5). Thus, we expect for example that it will successfully predict that the HSN lures will have higher false-alarm rates than the standard lures.

Third, and of greatest interest, the model potentially accounts for findings that old test probes with highly distinctive features may have elevated hit rates compared to old test probes without such features. Under the present formulation, both types of old test probes provide a perfect match to the memory trace that they produced so will yield identical P(Dj|Sj) values with respect to their matching trace in memory (Equation 3b). In the present formulation, the key to accounting for the elevated hit rates lies in the denominator of the likelihood-ratio corresponding to the matching trace, not the numerator. In particular, the probability that the new-item generation process will produce a memory trace with a highly distinctive feature is considerably lower than the probability that it will produce a memory trace without such a feature: the P(Dj|Nj) value will tend to be lower for high-distinctive memory traces than for low-distinctive ones (see Equation 6). Hence, the old/new likelihood ratio associated with the matching trace [P(Dj|Sj) /P(Dj|Nj) ] will be greater for memory traces with high distinctiveness. If the boost in the matching-trace likelihood ratio is sufficiently large, then the summed individual-trace old/new likelihood ratios (see Equation 2) may be greater for high-distinctive old test probes than for low-distinctive ones. The intuition here is that the memory system is concluding that the match of a test probe to a highly distinctive memory trace provides convincing evidence that the test probe must be old because there is a very low probability that the new-item generation process would have produced such a trace by chance alone.

We should remark that, even without making special provision for the role of distinctive features, the MDS-REM model might still have the needed machinery for predicting hit rate advantages for distinctive items. To the extent that such items lie in isolated regions of the MDS space, they will tend to yield small values of P(Dj|Nj), because their probability density in the continuous MDS space will be small in magnitude. However, we will see that making provision for the role of distinctive features allows MDS-REM to provide considerably better accounts of the present sets of old-new recognition data. Second, we should remark that whether MDS-REM predicts that high-distinctive items will have higher hit rates depends on the detailed structure of the MDS space in which the items are embedded and on parameter settings in the model.
