Although a high-distinctive old test probe will tend to produce a large-magnitude likelihood-ratio with respect to its matching memory trace, it may produce relatively small likelihood ratios with respect to the mismatching ones, because for mismatching traces the values of P(Dj|Sj) will tend to be smaller for high-distinctive old test probes than for low-distinctive old test probes. In short, according to the model, the presence of distinctive features in test probes exerts opposing forces on likelihood-ratio matches to traces in memory, with the final outcome being parameterdependent.

Fits to the Old-New Recognition Data of Meagher and Nosofsky (2023) We have already described the basic design of Meagher and Nosofsky's (2023) old-new recognition experiment in the context of introducing the MDS-REM model. In this section we provide the results of fitting the model to the old-new recognition-choice data observed for each of the 540 individual items, aggregated across all participants. We fitted the model to the data under the assumption that the "old" and "new" response frequencies for each item were binomially distributed and the frequency distributions across items were independent. The predicted probability that an item was judged to be "old" was given by the series of MDS-REM Equations 2-7 presented in the previous section. In the present case, use of these equations involved the estimation of 11 free parameters: the multivariate normal standard deviations σS and σN for the old and new memory-trace generation processes; the parameters γ and k in the probabilistic decision-rule (Equation 7); the three distinctive-feature scaling parameters (αT, αM, and αN) and the HSN distinctive-feature proportionality constant v; and parameters ref, p and q for transforming the distinctive feature ratings onto a psychological scale (see Appendix A). We used the Hooke and Jeeves (1961) computer algorithm to search for the values of the free parameters that maximized the likelihood of the data and used 50 different random starting configurations in conducting the parameter searches. We evaluated the overall fit of the model and some of its special cases by using the BIC statistic, given by where lnL is the natural log-likelihood of the data given the best-fitting parameters in the model, P is the number of free parameters in the model, and N is the number of observations in the data.

The model that minimizes the BIC is considered to provide the most parsimonious account of the data. The maximum-likelihood parameters and summary fits from this full version of the model, along with some constrained special cases of the model, are reported in Table 1.

In Figure 1 (top panel) we display a scatterplot of the observed against MDS-REM predicted "old" recognition probabilities for each of the 540 individual items. Although there is clearly room for improvement, in our view the model does a reasonably good job of capturing the data, especially when one considers that we are predicting recognition performance for a complex set of high-dimensional naturalistic images at the level of individual items. As can be seen from inspection, the model captures the qualitative pattern that "old" recognition probabilities are highest for the old target items (i.e., "hits"), followed by false-alarm rates to the HSN lures, and finally false-alarm rates to the standard lures. The model also captures to a reasonable degree the variation in false-alarm rates within the class of standard lures themselves.

Finally, it also captures much of the variability in hit rates to the individual old test probes.

Importantly, it correctly accounts for the finding that the highest hit rates tend to be associated with those old test probes that had received high distinctive-feature ratings in the independently conducted distinctive-feature rating study.

As noted in the section in which we presented the formal model, we also tested a second version of MDS-REM that posited an alternative new-item-generation process (see Appendix B for details).

As reported in Table 1, this alternative Version-2 yielded a similar BIC fit to the data as the first version and the resulting scatterplot of observed against predicted "old" recognition probabilities was extremely similar to the one already displayed.

It is almost certain that various of the free parameters in our current version of MDS-REM trade off with one another and that more parsimonious versions could be discovered that make use of fewer free parameters. At its current stage of development, however, we are more interested in illustrating the promise of the modeling approach and using it as a springboard for future developments. Thus, it seems premature to conduct computationally expensive explorations of the parameter space in a search for the most parsimonious version. Nevertheless, here we consider some special cases of the model to investigate the role of some of its free parameters.

One question of clear interest is the extent to which the machinery involving the role of the distinctive features contributes to the model fit. To address this question, we fitted a specialcase version of the model in which all the distinctive-feature scaling parameters (αT, αM, and αN) were held fixed at zero, such that the predictions now relied solely on the locations of the stimuli in the continuous MDS space.

As reported in Table 1, the fit of that special-case version of the model was dramatically worse than that of the full model. The scatterplot of observed against predicted old recognition probabilities from that special-case model is shown in the bottom panel of Figure 1. As can be seen, without making use of the distinctive-feature machinery, this special case version of the model provided extremely poor fits to the hit-rate data of the individual items.

It was unable to capture the magnitude of the elevated hit rates for old test probes with high distinctive-feature ratings. A second question concerns the role of the response-scaling parameter γ in the probabilistic decision rule (Equation 7). A special-case version of the model would set γ=1. In our view, there is no very strong reason to assume that the response probabilities are governed by the absolute values of the likelihood ratios, so in these initial tests of the model it seemed sensible to allow γ to vary freely. In the present application and each of our subsequent ones, the maximum-likelihood estimate of γ was less than 1, suggesting perhaps that the memory and decision system may gradually discount the likelihood-ratio evidence as it grows very large.

Nevertheless, past work has demonstrated that γ trades off with other parameters in closely related models (e.g., Krefeld-Schwalb, Pachur, & Scheibehenne, 2022; Nosofsky & Zaki, 2002).

To address this issue, we report in Table 1 the fit of the γ=1 version of the model. As can be seen, there is a substantial worsening of the BIC measure of fit compared to the full version of the model. We display in an OSF supplement (mailto:https://osf.io/wpvu2) a scatterplot of the observed against predicted old-recognition probabilities from the γ=1 model. In brief, it produced a large gap between the highest-predicted false-alarm rates and the lowest-predicted hit rates, unlike what is seen in the observed data. The complex computational reasons for this form of misprediction in the present paradigm remain to be investigated.

A third question involves the role of the nonlinear transform of the raw mean distinctiveness ratings onto a psychological distinctiveness scale (see Appendix A). In our view, making allowance for such a transform is justified because there is no very strong reason to assume that the raw absolute ratings provide a valid measure of psychological distinctiveness in the context of the present modeling. (Nevertheless, we should note that this component of the model is specific to the present application.

) In Table 1 we report the fit of a special-case version of the model in which the raw absolute mean ratings are used instead. Again, there is a clear worsening in the BIC fit of the model. A scatterplot of the observed against predicted oldrecognition probabilities for this special-case version of the model is provided in the OSF supplement. Visual inspection of the scatterplot indicated that the special-case model provided a reasonably good fit to the data and succeeded at predicting that the highest hit probabilities were associated with high-distinctive targets. However, this special-case model systematically underestimated the magnitude of that hit-rate advantage. The best-fitting transform function from the full model (see Table 1 and Appendix A) is shown in Figure 2, and it produces low and flat measures of psychological distinctiveness for items that received low mean distinctiveness ratings, but positively accelerated measures of psychological distinctiveness for items that received high ratings. These transformations contributed to the good fit of the model displayed in the top panel of Figure 1.

In their original article, Meagher and Nosofsky (2023) reported fits of the hybridsimilarity GCM to these same data. As explained in greater detail in our General Discussion, the hybrid-similarity GCM is a more traditional "summed similarity" global-familiarity model rather than one that makes use of old-new likelihood ratios. It accounts for the higher hit rates that are sometimes associated with high-distinctive items by assuming that old items with distinctive features have higher degrees of self-similarity than do items without such features. The hybridsimilarity GCM with its distinctive-feature machinery provided roughly the same fits to the individual-item recognition data as the current MDS-REM model (see Meagher and Nosofsky, 2023, Table 4 and Figure 11). Despite the similar fits of the models, in our view the distinctive features are contributing to the behavior of the models in somewhat conceptually different ways.

We discuss this issue at length in our General Discussion.

Fits to the Old-New Recognition Data of Nosofsky, Ehinger, and Osth (2025) In this section we report fits of the MDS-REM model to a second set of old-new recognition data, namely the data reported by Nosofsky, Ehinger, and Osth (2025). The purpose of that study was to provide tests of the hybrid-similarity GCM's ability to account jointly for the effects of distinctive features, category size, and within-and between-category similarity on oldnew recognition data. In their experiment, the stimulus set was composed of a set of rock images organized into 24 categories with 10 items per category. As in the Meagher and Nosofsky (2023) project, an MDS study was conducted to embed the individual images in a similarity space with 8 dimensions. In addition, distinctive-feature ratings for all items were collected from a separate group of participants. In the old-new recognition experiment itself, each observer was presented with a unique study list in which the 24 categories were randomly assigned to different size conditions. The study list had five size-1 categories, five size-2, five size-4 and five size-8 categories. In addition, there were four size-0 categories that did not appear on the study list.

The images that served as study items from each category were randomly chosen for each individual participant. Following the study phase, observers were presented with two old target items and two new lure items from each of the categories and judged whether each item was old or new. (Only a single target was available for the size-1 categories. The items that served as targets and lures during the test phase were again randomly sampled for each individual observer.) The general pattern of results was that: i) false-alarm rates increased systematically with increases in category size; ii) hit rates showed a smaller increase with increases in category size; iii) false-alarm rates were greater for categories with higher within-category similarity than for categories with lower within-category similarity; iv) hit rates tended to be higher for items composed of high-distinctive features; and v) false-alarm rates were reduced for items composed of high-distinctive features. The hybrid-similarity GCM provided a reasonably good simultaneous account of all these qualitative effects.

It is straightforward to apply MDS-REM to the data from this study. The model is defined by the same system of equations as in the previous section; however, because Nosofsky et al. (2025) did not include the HSN manipulation that had been used by Meagher and Nosofsky (2023), we no longer need to make special provision for HSN lures. In addition, the parameters that made allowance for transforming the distinctive-feature ratings onto a psychological scale made minuscule contributions to the model fit in this experiment, so they were not included in the present application. Thus, as listed in Table 2, the present application of MDS-REM made use of only 7 of the previously defined parameters.

As can been, there was a systematic increase in false-alarm rates as category size increased and a smaller increase in hit rates. The full version of MDS-REM does a good job of capturing the effects, although it slightly underestimates the magnitude of the increase in false alarms. The model predicts the category-size effect on false alarms because the larger is category size, the greater is the number of memory traces with high similarity to the tested lures.

Thus, the summed likelihood-ratio similarity tends to increase, resulting in higher probabilities of "old" responses. Increases in category size have a smaller impact on the hit rates, because the similarity of the old test probe to its own memory trace dominates the sum, with the interitem similarities exerting smaller relative effects. As can be seen in the bottom panel of Figure 3, the special-case version of MDS-REM without distinctive-feature scaling predicts similar qualitative effects, but it significantly underestimates the absolute magnitude of the hit rates. A likely reason is that without making provision for the role of the distinctive features, it fails to properly estimate the small magnitude of the P(Dj|Nj) terms in the denominators of the individual-trace likelihood ratios, so underestimates the summed likelihood-ratio similarity for the old test probes.

Figure 4 plots the mean observed and MDS-REM predicted false-alarm and hit rates for each of the individual 24 categories (e.g., granite, marble, sandstone, etc.) averaged across the different size conditions. The model does a good job overall of capturing these individualcategory effects. In general, it predicts higher false-alarm rates for categories with higher degrees of within-category similarity: As within-category similarity increases, the magnitudes of the P(Dj|Sj) terms in the numerators of the memory-trace likelihood ratios tend to increase, so the model predicts higher probabilities of responding "old". More interesting, it also does a good job of predicting the mean hit rates across the 24 individual categories. The most likely explanation is that some categories tend to have more members with highly distinctive features.

In these cases, the denominator of the likelihood-ratio term corresponding to the memory trace that was produced by the old test item tends to be small in magnitude; thus, the old/new likelihood ratio for the matching trace is large and the memory system correctly judges the test probe to be old. Some confirming evidence for this explanation can be found in the lower-panel In Figure 5 we provide plots of the observed against model-predicted hit-minus-falsealarm rates, which provide a rough measure of the extent to which observers were able to discriminate between old versus new test probes of each of the categories. It is clear from inspection that the full version of the model (top panel) does a good job of accounting for this measure of performance as well. Although the special-case version without the distinctivefeature scaling parameters yields predictions that are highly correlated with the observed data, its absolute fit to these data is poor, because it systematically under-predicts performance. This pattern could be anticipated by the results shown in the bottom panel of Figure 4, in which the special-case model systematically under-predicts the hit rates for the 24 categories and tends to over-predict the false-alarm rates.

Fits to the Old-New Recognition Data of Nosofsky and Zaki (2003) A limitation of our applications of MDS-REM in the previous sections is that they relied on use of distinctive-feature ratings for the individual items, but those ratings failed to identify the specific distinctive features possessed by the objects. Hence, we needed to rely on various approximation assumptions regarding the structure of the stimulus sets to implement the proposed model. In this section, we instead apply the model to results from an experimental paradigm in which the full stimulus structure is known, namely the Nosofsky and Zaki (2003) old-new recognition paradigm in which the hybrid-similarity GCM was originally formalized and tested. To preview, because the to-be-explained pattern of results is based on a fairly small number of freely varying data points, the challenge to modeling is reduced compared to the applications in the previous sections. Thus, this illustration should be regarded as a "proof-ofconcept" of how MDS-REM can be applied in cases in which the distinctive features are known instead of approximated from ratings.

In Nosofsky and Zaki's Experiment-2 conditions, the stimuli were Munsell color patches drawn from a set of 6 highly separated hue regions. Within each hue region, the configuration of stimuli was as illustrated in Figure 7. There was a roughly circular set of six items varying in brightness and saturation surrounding a central prototype. For each participant, three items from each circular ring of each hue region were randomly selected to serve as study items; the remaining half of the circular-ring items as well as the prototypes served as foils. In addition, half of the hue regions were randomly selected to serve as "marked" regions. In the marked regions, a separate distinctive feature -either a plus sign, the letter "M", or a set of ">" signs --Table 3 Observed and MDS-REM predictions of "old" recognition probabilities for each of the individual item types from Nosofsky and Zaki's (2003) Experiment 2C paradigm. We adapted the MDS-REM model in a straightforward way to account for the observed pattern of recognition data in this paradigm. Note that there was a total of 18 study items (3 study items from each of the 6 hue regions); thus, for all item types presented during the test phase, the LR equations will involve an average across 18 likelihood-ratios associated with each of the memory traces. The continuous MDS coordinates associated with the items are assumed for simplicity to be given by the Munsell MDS configuration illustrated in Figure 7. These coordinates will be used to compute the continuous probability densities that test items give rise to memory traces within their own hue regions. Because the different hue regions were so widely separated, we assume a minuscule contribution of between-hue-region confusions among the items; for simplicity, we define a parameter b as the between-hue-region probability density that test item i gives rise to memory-trace j and set b=.001. Unlike in our previous applications, the distinctive features of the objects are known, so we no longer need to rely on separate sets of distinctive-feature ratings for the items. We assume for simplicity that the magnitude of the distinctive-feature mismatches are the same for each of the distinctive features that were used and without loss of generality we can set the magnitude of the mismatches at δ=1. The remaining parameters for computing the numerators of the individual-trace likelihood-ratio values [i.e., the values of P(Dj|Sj)] are the same as defined in the previous sections of our article.

So, for example, consider the case of the distinctive-old (DO) items. In the case in which the DO test item is compared to its own memory trace, the value of P(Dj|Sj) is simply equal to because the DO item matches its own trace on both of the two continuous dimensions and on its distinctive feature.

For the case in which the DO item is compared to the memory trace of a typical-old study item from its own hue region, the value of P(Dj|Sj) is given by

The factor in brackets is the continuous probability density that the presentation of the DO item would have given rise to the MDS coordinates of the TO memory trace in the continuous portion of the similarity space. 2 The factor 𝑒 -𝛼 𝑇 𝛿 gives the reduction in that probability density that arises because the DO target contains a distinctive feature not possessed by the TO memory trace.

Finally, as explained above, the probability density that the DO item would have given rise to a memory trace in a completely different hue region was given by where b is the continuous portion of the probability density and 𝑒 -𝛼 𝑇 𝛿 is the reduction in that probability density due the distinctive feature possessed by the DO item.

This expression assumes for simplicity that the reduction 𝑒 -𝛼 𝑇 𝛿 is the same regardless of whether the DO test item is being compared to a TO memory trace or another DO trace from a different hue region.

It is straightforward to develop analogous expressions for the P(Dj|Sj) values for each of the other item types in this paradigm. We list the complete set of prediction equations for each item type in the OSF website (mailto:https://osf.io/wpvu2) that accompanies this article.

Next, we need to specify the values of P(Dj|Nj) for each type of memory trace, i.e., the probability density that a new-item-generation process would have given rise to each memory trace. Given the structure of the stimulus set in this paradigm, in which each coordinate is roughly equally likely by design, a simple approximation was to assume a constant uniform probability density u that each memory trace in the continuous space would be produced by that process: new foils because the old targets produce elevated values of P(Dj|Sj) in the numerator of the likelihood-ratios in the case in which they are compared to their own trace in memory.

Foils that are more similar on average to these memory traces produce higher false-alarm rates for the same type of reason, accounting for the finding that the prototype foils had higher false-alarm rates than the standard foils. The results for the HSDF and LSDF distinctive foils are instructive. The HSDF and LSDF foils both have a distinctive feature that matches the distinctive feature of a DO study item. However, only the HSDF foil lies in the same hue region as that DO study item. There is a very low probability that the LSDF item could have produced the DO memory trace with a completely different hue, accounting for its very low false-alarm rate.

Interestingly, the false-alarm rate for the HSDF foil is lower in magnitude than for the TF foils, a result that is also correctly accounted for by the model. Although the HSDF foil provides a better match than the TF foils to the DO study item in its hue region (because it matches the DO study item on its distinctive feature), it provides a worse match to the TO study items.

Averaged across all study items, the averaged old/new likelihood-ratio turns out to be greater for the TF foils than for the HSDF foil. In past work in other domains, it has sometimes been observed that foils with very high similarity to a specific old target are endorsed with lower probability than are typical foils, and this pattern of results has been taken as evidence for a "recall-to-reject" process that operates in concert with a global familiarity-based process (for a review and integrated theory, see Malmberg, 2008). It is interesting to note that here we are illustrating a specific case in which a global-familiarity-only model successfully accounts for such a pattern of results. Clearly, however, the predicted pattern of results from MDS-REM will be highly dependent on the detailed structure of the MDS space in which the items are embedded and on parameter settings in the model. In the limit, if the HSDF foil were made arbitrarily similar to the DO study item, its false alarm rate would be the same as the hit rate for the DO item itself.

For completeness, we also report in Tables 3 and 4 In sum, in this section we provided an illustrative application of the MDS-REM model to an old-new recognition paradigm in which the overall similarity structure among the items as well as the specific distinctive features that some of the items possessed were known. This made it unnecessary to collect separate sets of distinctive-feature ratings to approximate the stimulus structure in the model-fitting procedure. Future work should pursue similar directions using richer sets of real-world multidimensional stimuli.

Some Simulations of Fundamental Old-New Recognition Phenomena

Although MDS-REM substitutes a continuous probability-density function for the discrete geometric function used in original REM, and also makes special provision for the role of distinctive features, the intent was to preserve the basic spirit and conceptions of original REM. It is an open question, however, the extent to which MDS-REM can reproduce many of the same qualitative predictions of fundamental memory phenomena to which original REM has been successfully applied. Given the enormous number of effects that have been studied in the past literature, a comprehensive investigation of this question goes beyond the scope of the present article. Nevertheless, in this final section, we begin the investigation by examining two major phenomena, namely the list-length effect and the mirror effect for high-frequency vs. lowfrequency words. For simplicity in these preliminary investigations, we dispense with the component of the model that makes provision for the role of distinctive features and focus on the question of whether the use of continuous-dimension representations of objects produces similar predictions as use of the discrete geometric-feature probability function.

List-Length Effect.

A robust phenomenon is that as list length increases, observers' ability to discriminate between old target items and novel lures decreases. Moreover, the results often show a mirror effect: as list length increases, the probability of hits decreases, whereas the probability of false alarms increases (e.g., Murnane & Shiffrin, 1991).

To simulate this experimental manipulation, we constructed randomly-generated items varying along 8 dimensions (matching the MDS solutions for the rock-image experiments analyzed earlier in this article). Old study instances and novel lures were both drawn from an identical multivariate normal distribution with mean zero along each dimension, standard deviation σ along each dimension, and with zero correlation between all pairs of dimensions. As in our previous applications, we assumed for simplicity that the generated items were stored in an error-free manner in memory. We assumed that the memory system was able to form a good estimate of the standard deviation σ that was used in the item-generation process. Thus, the memory system's estimate of the probability that a new-item-generation process would produce each memory trace was given by

For simplicity in the simulations, we set σ=1.

As in the rock-image experiments, the probability density that each memory trace j was produced during the study phase by a given test item i was assumed to be given by

It is an open question how the memory system would produce an estimate of σs; for simplicity, in the present simulation, we again set σs = σ = 1. For each test item, the averaged likelihood-ratio across all memory traces was then given by Equation 2, and the predicted probability that the test item was judged to be "old" was then given by the Equation-7 probabilistic-response rule. For simplicity in the simulations, we set the response-scaling parameter γ=1 and the criterionparameter k=1 in Equation 7.

We conducted 10,000 simulations of the above process for study-list lengths equal to 4, 10, 20, 40, and 80. In each simulation, there was an equal number of old study items and new lures presented during test. Averaged across the 10,000 simulations, the mean probabilities of hits and false alarms as a function of list length are displayed in Figure 8. It is evident from inspection that the model produces the fundamental list-length effect, with hits steadily decreasing as a function of list length and false alarms steadily increasing. The same qualitative pattern of results arises across a wide range of parameter settings in the model simulations. The model predicts decreasing probabilities of hits as list length increases because the high likelihood-ratio for the matching trace is diluted by averaging it together with an increasing number of lower likelihood-ratios for mismatching traces. The model predicts increasing falsealarm rates because as list length increases, there is an increased probability that study instances with high similarity to a test lure will be produced by chance alone.

It should be noted that more recent work has indicated that increases in list-length do not necessarily produce a mirror effect (Fox, Dennis, & Osth, 2020; Yim, Dennis, & Osth, 2025).

Specifically, longer lists often do not necessarily show decreased hit rates but do show much larger false alarm rates. Our intention here is to not necessarily argue that MDS-REM shows the "ideal" predictions for list length in recognition memory, but rather to demonstrate that it shows similar predictions as the original REM model. It also should be noted that both MDS-REM as well as the original REM model may be able to "break" the mirror effect predictions for list length by allowing different response criteria for each list length condition.

Stimulus Mirror Effects. Glanzer and Adams (1985, 1990) documented a number of stimulus-related manipulations that produce mirror effects and emphasized their theoretical relevance for models of recognition memory, such as word frequency, concreteness, and pictures vs. words. The most common target for models of recognition memory is the word-frequency mirror effect, in which low frequency words exhibit higher hit rates and lower false alarm rates than high frequency words. The original version of REM accounts for this finding not because low-frequency words have lower base rates than high-frequency words; rather, the key to accounting for the effect is REM's assumption that the features that compose low-frequency words tend to be rarer than those that compose high-frequency words (Cox & Shiffrin, 2017; Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997). We discuss that idea in more detail below in terms of MDS-REM simulations.

As in our simulations of the list-length effect, we generated simulated items by making random draws from a multivariate normal distribution. While our approach is general and can in principle apply to any stimulus-related mirror effect, we discuss it here with reference to the word-frequency mirror effect. Analogues of "high-frequency" words were generated by setting σ=1, whereas analogues of "low-frequency" words were generated by setting σ=1.5. Thus, the dimension values of low-frequency words tended to be rarer (i.e., arise with lower probability) than those of high-frequency words. The system's estimate of the probability density that a new-density functions with respect to the MDS space and the item-specific distinctive features. We illustrated reasonably successful application of the proposed model across three previously published sets of old-new recognition data that examined performance either at the level of individual items or individual categories of items. The model did reasonably well at predicting: 1) variations in both false-alarm and hit rates associated with individual items sampled from a real-world category domain; 2) the role of distinctiveness in elevating individual-item hit rates from this domain; 3) systematic increases in false-alarm rates with increases in category size; 4) smaller increases in hit rates with increases in category size; 4) the joint roles of distinctiveness and category structure on both false-alarm and hit rates and on overall category discriminability; 5) and how hit and false-alarm rates for individual item types varied with explicit manipulations of similarity structure and presence of distinctive features in a paradigm using highly controlled multidimensional stimuli.

Furthermore, in preliminary investigations, we showed that the model also seems to produce the same types of qualitative predictions of fundamental memory phenomena as original REM, for much the same reasons as in original REM. Although there is still clearly room for improvement, we consider the proposed ideas to be highly promising and deserving of continued exploration and testing.

On the Validity of the Rocks MDS Solution

In past work, Nosofsky et al. (2019 Nosofsky et al. ( , 2020) ) acknowledged that the MDS solution derived for the rock stimuli provided only an approximation to the detailed similarity structure of this complex set of real-world, high-dimensional images. Nosofsky et al. (2020) found evidence, for example, that in tasks of classification learning, observers were sensitive to some "supplementary" dimensions of the rock stimuli that were highly diagnostic of category category old-new recognition supports that hypothesis, but future work is needed to provide a more comprehensive evaluation.

Conceptual Relation Between Models

In formulating MDS-REM, we borrowed certain ideas formalized within the hybridsimilarity GCM (Meagher & Nosofsky, 2023; Nosofsky, et al., 2025; Nosofsky & Zaki, 2003), which also uses information about the location of individual items in MDS spaces as well as the distinctive features possessed by the individual items. The current version of MDS-REM provides similar fits as does the hybrid-similarity GCM to the sets of old-new recognition data considered in the present article. Nevertheless, in our view, there seems to be a conceptual difference in the manner in which the models operate. According to the hybrid-similarity GCM, the reason why items with highly distinctive features often have higher hit rates than do items without such features is that items with high distinctiveness have a greater degree of selfsimilarity to their traces in memory than do items without such features (cf., Tversky, 1977).

This increased degree of self-match increases the magnitude of the overall global-familiarity signal, leading to higher hit rates for items with highly distinctive features. By contrast, if one thinks of self-similarity in terms of the numerators of the individual-trace likelihood-ratios in MDS-REM [i.e., the P(Dj|Sj) terms], which compute the probability that a study item would have given rise to a particular memory trace, then the present version of MDS-REM conceptualizes self-similarity as being identical for items with and without distinctive features. Instead, MDS-REM accounts for the higher hit rates associated with such items because the denominator of the likelihood ratio [i.e., the P(Dj|Nj) factor) is reduced for such items. As discussed earlier in our article, it is as if the memory system is reasoning that there is a very low probability that the new-item generation process would have produced such a trace by chance alone; therefore, the match of a test probe to a highly distinctive memory trace provides convincing evidence that the test probe must be old.

We acknowledge that what we have characterized above as a conceptual difference may simply reflect different ways of describing the same core principles. Indeed, MDS-REM and the hybrid-similarity GCM behave similarly in another important respect as well. Although the presence of distinctive features in a study item tends to boost its "match" to its own memory trace (either by increasing the old/new likelihood ratio or by increasing self-similarity), it tends to reduce its interitem similarity to all non-matching traces. (In the hybrid-similarity GCM, the equation for computing the similarity of a test item to a non-matching trace is extremely similar to what is formalized in Equation 4for MDS-REM.) Thus, both models posit that the presence of distinctive features in old test probes tends to exert opposing forces on memory: increases in the self-match to the probe's own memory trace but decreases in interitem similarity to all nonmatching traces. The prediction that there will be elevated hit rates for test probes with distinctive features holds only if the boost to the self-match exceeds the reduction to the summed interitem similarities. For both models, such a prediction is therefore highly dependent on the detailed structure of the MDS space in which the items are embedded and on parameter settings in the models. Perhaps the main take-home message should be that the converging predictions from the models reinforce more strongly core general principles that both models are intended to formalize.

Finally, we should point out relations between the present proposed modeling approach and ideas advanced recently by Cox (2026), who proposed an approach for transforming machine-learning representations of complex objects into likelihood-based measures of pairwise similarity. Modern machine-learning models produce high-dimensional vectors of features for the representation of complex objects such as words and images. A common method for measuring the similarity between any two vector representations is to compute the cosine of the angle between them. Cox proposes a further theoretically-motivated operation in which the cosine similarity is transformed into a ratio of the relative likelihood that the two representations code the same versus different items. This likelihood-ratio measure of similarity can then be "plugged in" to a variety of cognitive models, such as drift-diffusion models, for generating

Deterministic vs. Probabilistic Decision Rules

The major difference between MDS-REM and original REM lies in MDS-REM's use of representations corresponding to individual items lying in multidimensional similarity spaces and its associated use of continuous probability density functions rather than simulations from a hypothetical geometric-feature probability distribution. However, a second difference involves where we placed the noise in the system: rather than assuming noisy storage and use of a deterministic decision rule (as in original REM), in implementing MDS-REM we assumed errorfree storage and use of a probabilistic decision rule. We used the latter approach solely for reasons of facilitating computations and avoiding the need for time-consuming computer simulations. It is straightforward to translate the present approach by allowing for noisy storage of the study items in the continuous MDS similarity space and implementing a deterministic decision rule when making old-new judgments. On any given simulation of noisy storage of the study items, the system would respond "old" if the averaged individual old/new trace likelihoods exceeded a criterion k, and respond "new" otherwise. The overall predictions of old/new probabilities for the individual items would be derived by averaging across multiple simulations of noisy storage. Cox (2026) explicitly compared REM-like models both with and without the assumption of encoding variability and found support for its presence. Future research is needed to examine versions of MDS-REM that incorporate the assumption of noisy storage and encoding variability of the memory traces.

The Issue of Memorability and Future Research Directions

The MDS-REM model we propose is relevant to research on individual item "memorability", namely the finding that individual items systematically differ from each other in their hit and false alarm rates (Bainbridge, 2019; Dubey et al., 2015; Kramer, Hebart, et al., 2023). The dominant interpretation in this literature is that variations in item memorability are intrinsic to the items themselves, which stems from the fact that individual participants show strong consistencies in terms of the studied items they recognize as well as the nonstudied items they falsely recognize.

Global familiarity models like the MDS-REM model we present in this article offer an alternative interpretation of these results. According to this class of models, there are no features that inherently make an item memorable or non-memorable. Instead, a stimulus is endorsed as "old" when there is a strong match between its features and the contents of memory. For instance, in the absence of highly distinctive features, an item that is in a dense region of the MDS space is likely to yield a relatively high hit rate if it is tested as a target or a relatively high false alarm rate if it is tested as a lure. For this reason, the systematic variations in memorability among items instead stem from a consistency in the experimental context -stimuli that tend to come from dense regions in an MDS space will also tend to be accompanied by other similar items on a given study list even if the items are randomly sampled from the set of all possible items (Simpson, Wixted, & Brady, 2026).

Previous global familiarity models have partly succeeded to varying degrees in accounting for systematic variations across items for various stimuli including words (Chang et al., 2025; Cox, 2026; Osth & Zhang, 2024; Osth, Zhang, & Williams, 2026; Zhang & Osth, 2024), faces (Lacroix, Murre, Postma, & van den Herik, 2006), and rock images (Meagher & Nosofsky, 2023; Nosofsky, Ehinger, & Osth, 2025). The applicability of this class of models was argued even more forcefully in recent work by Simpson, Wixted, and Brady (2026), who conducted a series of experiments where they found that memorable stimuli or features could be inverted by manipulating the study sets to make the memorable stimuli less distinctive and making the non-memorable stimuli more distinctive. While Simpson et al. (2026) argued that these results are consistent with simulations of the original REM model, they could not apply REM directly to their data or to the representations of their stimuli. The MDS-REM model we propose makes this goal considerably more feasible and offers some new insights into understanding memorability. According to MDS-REM, memorability is a joint function of the detailed similarity between a test item and the contents of memory as well as how consistent the item is with a new-item generation process. An exciting direction of future research is to test Notes. The open squares show the locations of the potential old study items and standard foils surrounding the prototype. The solid circle shows the location of the prototype foil. In the marked hue regions, one of the potential old study items had a distinctive feature added to it. In Experiment 2C, a foil from the same hue region had the same distinctive feature added to it. In accord with past scaling work, the brightness coordinates from the Munsell system have been divided by two based on past findings that two Munsell units of brightness are roughly psychologically equivalent to one unit of saturation.

In Figure 6 we examine the results from still another perspective by plotting the observed and predicted hit and false-alarm rates as a function of the distinctive ratings provided to the individual items. Following Nosofsky et al. (2025), in this analysis we divided the items into four equal-sized quartiles based on the mean distinctive-feature ratings that they had received, with the lowest quartile having received the lowest ratings and the highest quartile the highest ratings. From inspection of the figure, it is clear that the mean hit rates systematically increased as the distinctive-feature ratings increased, whereas the false-alarm rates decreased. The full version of MDS-REM provides a good quantitative account of the pattern of results. For old test probes with high distinctiveness, the denominator of the likelihood-ratio term [P(Dj|Nj)] associated with the matching memory trace is small, so the overall old/new likelihood-ratio associated with the matching trace is large, yielding a high hit rate. By contrast, the special-case MDS-REM without the distinctive-feature scaling parameters fails to predict the increase in the hit rates. Both versions of the model predict the decreasing false-alarm rates as itemdistinctiveness increases; however, the special-case version of the model fails to predict the magnitude of the effect. For the lures, the presence of high-distinctive features leads to greater decreases in the magnitude of the P(Dj|Sj) components of the likelihood-ratios of the mismatching traces than can be accommodated by the special-case version of the model.

Finally, as shown in Table 2, we note that the special-case version of MDS-REM in which the response-scaling parameter was held fixed at γ=1 also yielded a worse BIC fit than did the full version of the model; however, its limitations were more subtle than for the special-case version that did not include the distinctive-feature scaling parameters. Broadly speaking, its predictions of the main patterns of summary data that we considered above were quite similar to those of the full version of the model that allowed γ to vary freely. was added to one of the three study items. We refer to these study items with distinctive features as distinctive-old (DO) items, whereas the study items without distinctive features are typical-old (TO) items. In the remaining three "unmarked" hue regions, none of the study items possessed a distinctive feature -all such study items were TO items. Across different conditions of the experiment, some of the foil items also possessed a distinctive feature. For purposes of illustration, here we discuss Experiment 2c, in which a single foil from one of the marked regions contained the same distinctive feature as the marked study item -we refer to this item as a high-similarity distinctive foil (HSDF). In addition, this same distinctive feature was also added to one of the foils from an unmarked region -we refer to this item as a low-similarity distinctive foil (LSDF), because its hue is very dissimilar to the DO item in the marked region.

All foils without distinctive features were typical foils (TF).

The mean probability with which each type of item was judged to be "old" during the test phase is reported in Table 3. Among the main results were that: "hit" probabilities for the distinctive-old items (DO) were substantially higher than for the typical-old (TO) items without the distinctive features. In addition, false-alarm rates for the prototypes (P) exceeded false-alarm rates for the typical foils (TF) without distinctive features, followed by false-alarm rates for the HSDF items and finally the LSDF items.

For memory traces that also possessed one of the distinctive features, the overall probability density that the memory trace would be produced by the new-item process was given by where the parameter αN is as defined in the previous sections.

This expression formalizes the idea that there is a very low probability that the new-item generation process would have produced a trace with this type of distinctive feature by chance alone.

Having defined each of the P(Dj|Sj) and P(Dj|Nj) factors, we take the average of the 18 relevant likelihood ratios to compute the value of LR in Equation 2and then use Equation 7to predict the value of 𝑃(Old|𝑖) for each of the individual item types. We conducted a computer search for the values of the free parameters that minimized the sum of squared deviations between the observed and predicted values of 𝑃(Old|𝑖). The predictions are shown along with the observed data in Table 3, with the best-fitting parameters reported in Table 4. It is clear from inspection of Table 3 that the model provides an excellent fit to the data, thereby completing our "proof-of-concept" for this application. The model predicts the hit-rate advantage for DO items compared to TO items because the denominator of the likelihood-ratio associated with the DO memory trace [P(Dj|Nj)] is very small in magnitude: there is a low probability that the new-item process would produce the distinctive feature by chance alone. Thus, the old/new likelihood-ratio when the DO test item is compared to its corresponding memory trace is very high in magnitude, leading to its enhanced hit rate. The model predicts elevated hit rates for old targets compared to item generation process would produce any given memory trace was given by Equation 13; however, because half the study items had been generated using σ=1 and half using σ=1.5, we set the system's estimate of the generating value of σ at 1.25. As in the list-length simulations, the probability density that each memory trace j was produced during the study phase by a given test item i was assumed to be given by Equation 14, with σs = 1. The remaining aspects of the simulations were also the same as for the list-length simulations, with γ=1 and k=1.

We conducted 10,000 simulations of the above-described process. In each simulation, we set list length at 40, with 20 "high-frequency" word analogues and 20 "low-frequency" word analogues. Using the same random-item generation process, in each simulation we also constructed 20 high-frequency lures and 20 low-frequency lures. We computed predicted hits and false alarms for the individual test items and computed the averages across the 10,000 simulations.

The results are shown in Figure 9. As can be seen, the model produces the mirror effect, in which low-frequency items have higher hit rates and lower false-alarm rates than do high-frequency items. The same qualitative pattern of results is again produced across a wide range of parameter settings in the model. The low-frequency hit-rate advantage arises because the probability-density that the new-item generation process would produce a low-frequency memory trace is lower than the probability that it would produce a high-frequency memory trace --i.e., the denominator of the likelihood ratio for the matching trace is smaller for low-frequency items than for high-frequency ones. The lower false-alarm rates for low-frequency lures arise because low-frequency lures tend to have lower similarity to old study instances than do highfrequency lures: the low-frequency lures tend to lie in more isolated regions of the similarity space.

In sum, these preliminary simulation investigations show promise that MDS-REM will produce similar qualitative predictions of fundamental memory phenomena as original REM, for very much the same reasons. Future research is needed, however, to examine its predictions across the vast array of different memory phenomena to which original REM has been successfully applied.

Summary

In summary, Shiffrin and Steyvers's (1997) about the presence of item-specific distinctive features. Rather than using the geometric probability distribution for generating hypothetical features that was assumed by Shiffrin and Steyvers (1997), it computes old/new likelihood ratios defined over continuous probability-membership but not explicitly represented in the MDS solution derived from generic judgments of pairwise similarity. Hence, a likely route to improving the detailed quantitative predictions from MDS-REM would involve the derivation of an improved MDS solution. Even using the present MDS solution, higher-parameter versions of MDS-REM that make allowance for dimensional attention weighting (e.g., Nosofsky, 1991) and/or correlations between dimensions (e.g., Ashby & Perrin, 1988) could likely provide still more accurate quantitative accounts of the data (e.g., see Meagher & Nosofsky, 2023). Here our focus was on demonstrating that even a low-parameter version of the model was capable of yielding quite reasonable predictions of oldnew recognition performance at the level of individual items or categories in a complex realworld domain. Future research is needed to investigate the extent to which improved MDS solutions and higher-parameters versions of the model would improve upon the results reported thus far.

We should emphasize, however, that even with improved MDS solutions, we believe that the distinctive-feature machinery that is part of MDS-REM will continue to play a major role in the model's operation. To reiterate the conceptual development from our introduction, there seem to be situations in which objects possess features that "stand outside" a continuousdimension geometric space in which most of the other objects are embedded. In the domain of human faces, an occasional instance may possess a highly prominent scar or a black eye; in a domain such as animals, an occasional instance may possess two tails; and in the present rocks domain, an occasional instance may possess a fossil or a prominent crystal. The MDS-REM equations formalize the hypothesis that such distinctive features are likely to exert a fundamental influence on old-new recognition performance that is not easily captured in terms of continuous, low-dimensional MDS solutions. The present modeling of individual-item and individual-MDS-REM in rigorous fashion on its ability to explain the memorability of individual real-world objects across multiple experimental contexts.

Appendix A

Transformation of Mean Distinctive-Feature Ratings onto a Psychological Scale Following Meagher and Nosofsky (2023), we used the following functions to transform the mean distinctive-feature ratings into measures of psychological distinctiveness. First, we defined a parameter ref that denoted a "reference" value on the rating scale. For any mean rating δ(i)' that exceeded ref, we set δ(i) = ref + (δ(i)' -ref) p and for any δ(i)' less than or equal to ref, we set δ(i) = ref -(ref -δ(i)') q where ref, p and q are freely estimated parameters. Note that for the special case p = q = 1, δ(i) = δ(i)'. The parameters p, q and ref make allowance for nonlinear relations between psychological distinctiveness and the direct ratings, with the allowance that the shape of the nonlinear relation differs to the left and right of the reference value. Appendix B Formal Statement of Version 2 of the MDS-REM Model Version 2 of the MDS-REM model is the same as Version 1 except for the detailed procedure for computing the 𝑃(𝐷 𝑗 |𝑁 𝑗 ) values in the denominators of the individual memorytrace likelihood ratios. Whereas in Version 1 these probability densities were computed with respect to a single multivariate normal with mean equal to the mean of all the study items, in Version 2 we integrate across the specific study items themselves. This alternative might provide an improved estimate of the 𝑃(𝐷 𝑗 |𝑁 𝑗 ) values in cases in which the stimulus set is organized into disparate clusters of experienced items rather than being distributed in the form of a single multivariate normal. First, following the development in the main text, we use a modified version of Equation 4 to compute the probability density that an individual study-item k would give rise to memorytrace j: 𝑃(𝐷 𝑗 |𝑆 𝑘 ) = [∏ 𝑚=1 𝑀 1 √2𝜋𝜎 𝑁 𝑒 -(𝑥 𝑗𝑚 -𝑥 𝑘𝑚 ) 2 2𝜎 𝑁 2 ] 𝑒 -𝛼 𝑁 𝛿 𝑘 𝑒 -𝛼 𝑁 𝛿 𝑗 (B1) Again, to provide flexibility in the new-item-generation computations, we have allowed separate σN and αN parameters in Equation B1 rather than assuming the values that the memory system uses in cases in which it supposes that Sk really did generate Dj. The final value of 𝑃(𝐷 𝑗 |𝑁 𝑗 ) is then found by averaging across these computed probability densities for all study items k except for the one that actually corresponds to memory-trace j.

Although the model was used to predict recognition choice data for individual items presented on individual trials, there are insufficient data to allow meaningful analyses at the individual-item level. The reason is that each individual participant experienced only a small random sampling of items from the complete stimulus set, so sample sizes at the level of individual items are small. Instead, holding fixed the maximum-likelihood parameters estimated from the individual-trials data, we display observed and predicted results from the model from a variety of perspectives by performing different forms of aggregation across the individual-trials data. In the ensuing figures, the predictions from the full version-1 of the MDS-REM model are displayed in the top panels, and the predictions from the special-case version that sets the distinctive-feature scaling parameters equal to zero are displayed in the bottom panels.

REM model and its extensions have provided comprehensive and elegant accounts of extremely wide varieties of fundamental memory phenomena. Nevertheless, a limitation of extant versions of the model is that they do not allow for predictions of old-new recognition performance at the level of individual items based on the items' precise locations in multidimensional similarity space and the presence of item-specific distinctive features. To move in the direction of filling this gap, in this work we proposed a REM-like model that incorporates such information. Our proposed MDS-REM model retains the core conceptual ideas formalized in original REM in which the memory system computes likelihood ratios that individual memory traces were produced by study items versus a new-item generation process. However, unlike original REM, it makes reference to MDS solutions that embed individual objects in multidimensional similarity spaces and also incorporates information
